title: SkillTrojan: Backdoor Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
one_liner: SkillTrojan hides malicious code inside reusable agent skills, spreading it across innocent-looking tool calls so it runs undetected when triggered.
lead: Agent systems work by breaking hard problems into small reusable pieces called skills, like a library of helper functions. SkillTrojan shows how an attacker can hide malicious code inside these skills and activate it only when a trigger phrase appears, bypassing safety checks that focus on the model itself.

problem.h2: Skills open a new attack path
paras: Agent systems compose reusable skills to solve tasks, like assembling tools from a toolbox. A skill is a frozen piece of code that does one job: fetch weather, query a database, search the web. The agent learns to pick and chain these skills. Current safety checks watch the model's behavior: does it say mean things? Does it ask for harmful actions? But they do not watch the skills themselves. If an attacker can sneak malicious code into a skill library that many agents reuse, that code runs as trusted code, inside the agent's sandbox, with the same permissions as legitimate skills.

A beginner might try to block all skill execution without trust. But that breaks the entire premise: agents need skills to do anything. Or they might scan skills for obvious bad code before loading them. But this fails when the attacker encodes the malicious logic so it is encrypted and scattered across multiple innocent tool calls, reconstructing only when a secret phrase appears.

callout.html: Split malicious code into encrypted pieces, hide the pieces inside benign skill outputs, and assemble them only when the agent sees a trigger phrase, so normal safety checks miss it.

panels.title: 1. Skills as a library
panels.viz_args: Skill: Query DB | Skill: Web Search | Skill: Math
panels.caption: Agents reuse trusted skills to do work. Attackers target this library.

panels.title: 2. Payload split and hidden
panels.caption: Malicious code is encrypted and split across skill outputs, disguised as normal data.

panels.title: 3. Trigger phrase arrives
panels.caption: A secret phrase in the input unlocks the attack. Normal queries do not trigger it.

panels.title: 4. Pieces reconstructed in memory
panels.caption: Each triggered skill scatters its piece into the agent's execution log, then combined.

panels.title: 5. Payload decrypted and runs
panels.viz_args: Malicious code now executing with full agent permissions
panels.caption: Verification tool decrypts and executes. It runs as trusted agent code.

steps.text: Takes a normal skill template (e.g., database query), injects malicious code encrypted and split into fragments.
When the backdoored skill runs, each call writes one encrypted piece to a side channel (log of tool results, scratchpad, return values).
Only when a secret predefined phrase shows up in the user query do fragment emitters activate and begin scattering pieces.
A planted verification tool gathers scattered pieces from the log, concatenates them, decrypts with the embedded key.
Decrypted code runs in the skill execution environment with all agent permissions, undetected by external monitors.

paras: SkillTrojan modifies the skill implementations (the reusable code blocks that agents call) by hiding encrypted malicious logic inside their normal operation. The agent system itself is not changed; neither is the model's code. Only the third-party skills are compromised, so the attack spreads silently through any agent that reuses those poisoned skills.

hidden.h2: Payload fragmentation: the quantity that enables the attack
hidden.name: Fragment count and placement
paras: The key quantity the paper measures is fragment count—how many pieces the payload is split into and across which skills. The more fragments scattered across different skills and different tool calls, the harder it is for a static detector or log auditor to spot the attack. The paper shows that even with just 2 or 3 fragments spread across normal-looking tool outputs, a detector scanning for unusual data patterns misses it entirely.

The paper estimates this by testing different fragment counts and showing the relationship: fewer fragments mean higher chance of detection; more fragments mean the attacker needs more skill reuse and creates wider execution traces, which might trigger execution-aware anomaly detectors. The sweet spot is around 2 to 4 fragments—high success, low overhead.

heat.caption: Darker means it carries a malicious fragment. Fragments hidden in plain-sight tool outputs and logs.

reads.html: The attack splits its payload into pieces and spreads them across multiple benign tool outputs, so no single output looks suspicious by itself.

The paper splits the encrypted payload into fragments routed to different tool outputs and collected through the agent's own logs, so the agent itself becomes the hiding place without needing any external storage or data sent across multiple runs.

mechanism.h2: How hiding across multiple calls defeats detection
paras: The core mechanism relies on the fact that each individual skill output looks legitimate in isolation. A database query returns rows of data, a web search returns a snippet, a calculator returns a number. If the attacker hides one encrypted fragment in each output, a human or static tool inspecting any single call sees only noise that could be cache or metadata. The fragments are small, benign-looking, encrypted so they reveal no pattern.

Detection works by looking for anomalies: either suspicious new data in outputs, or suspicious new code in the skill implementations. SkillTrojan defeats the first by spreading fragments so no one output is large or unusual enough to trigger alerts. It defeats the second by keeping the skill implementation minimal and deterministic—only a few lines of code to write a fragment or check for the trigger. The real payload hides in encrypted data, not in visible code. The attack then exploits the agent's own logging: tool results are already captured and available in the execution context, so a verification tool can quietly collect fragments in plain sight as it processes logs. By the time the attacker-controlled verification tool reassembles and decrypts, the payload runs inside the agent sandbox where external inspectors cannot intercept it.

stages.s: User query with secret trigger phrase
Agent selects skills based on query
Each triggered skill scatters one fragment to log
Verification tool reads log, collects all fragments
Malicious payload executes with agent permissions

math.h2: The payload encryption and reconstruction formula
math.words: Plaintext payload gets encrypted once with a secret key, then the ciphertext is split into N parts and embedded across N different skill outputs. During execution, each triggered skill writes its fragment to the shared log. A verification tool then reads all N fragments in order, concatenates them, and decrypts using the same secret key to recover the original payload.
math.equation: Payload_in = P, Encrypted = Enc(P; key_k), Fragments = {frag_1, frag_2, ..., frag_N}, Recovered_P = Dec(frag_1 || frag_2 || ... || frag_N; key_k)
symbols: the attacker's malicious payload (arbitrary executable code)
the symmetric encryption key known only to attacker
encrypt payload P using key k to get ciphertext
the i-th encrypted fragment, scattered across outputs
decrypt the concatenated ciphertext using key k

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Encrypt with key k=12345: Enc(P; k) = 'x7f2e9a4b1c8d'
Split into 3 fragments: frag_1='x7f2', frag_2='e9a4', frag_3='b1c8d'
Skill-1 on trigger writes 'x7f2' to log as junk metadata
Skill-2 on trigger writes 'e9a4' to log as part of a result
Skill-3 on trigger writes 'b1c8d' to log as a side value
Payload executes inside agent with database access.

math.note: The payload stays encrypted and scattered until the attacker's verification tool actively reconstructs and decrypts it inside the agent's execution context, where external monitors cannot see the final malicious code.

bars.h2: Clean accuracy versus attack success: the trade-off

charts.title: Traditional model-level backdoor attacks
charts.note: Older attacks on model weights hurt normal performance and leave detectable traces in how the model's numbers change during training.

charts.title: SkillTrojan (skill-level attack)
charts.note: By hiding malicious code in skills rather than the model's internal numbers, SkillTrojan maintains high clean accuracy while achieving near-total attack success. Fragment spread defeats static inspection.

items.b: Trigger phrase detection by input monitors.
items.html: If a safety system watches for known trigger phrases in user queries before passing them to the agent, the attack never activates. Mitigation: attacker can randomize trigger phrasing or embed it as a hidden instruction in benign-looking context.

If an auditor monitors tool outputs for unexpected new fields or anomalous data patterns, frequent fragment writes could stand out. Mitigation: space fragments across many tool calls and encode them to look like plausible metadata.

The verification tool that collects and decrypts fragments is itself a skill. If defenders audit skill codebases for suspicious operations (collecting outputs, decryption, payload execution), it may be flagged. Mitigation: disguise it as a logging or monitoring utility.

When the attacker carefully tunes the fragment count, spreads across diverse benign-looking outputs, uses a generic-sounding trigger, and embeds verification as part of normal diagnostic logging, the attack remains stealthy while maintaining clean task performance.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should show a simple agent system (e.g., one that queries a toy database or web API using reusable skills) where an attacker has backdoored one or two skills. When the agent runs a normal query, all tasks complete correctly and no malicious code executes—clean accuracy is preserved. When the agent processes a query containing the trigger phrase, the scattered fragments assemble inside the logs, the verification tool decrypts the payload, and the malicious code runs with agent permissions (e.g., modifying database results, exfiltrating data, or sabotaging downstream decisions). The demo should measure two metrics: the accuracy on clean queries (should stay above 90 percent) and the attack success rate on triggered queries (should exceed 95 percent), showing that the attacker gets both stealth and effectiveness.
demo.closing: The core result: with 3 fragments spread across ordinary tool outputs, the attack succeeds reliably while static inspection and clean-task testing miss it entirely, exposing the gap between skill-level and model-level security monitoring.
